The pilot did not correct for wind, effectively homing toward the NAVAID without maintaining the required runway heading. The deviation was corrected once the radio issue was resolved.

text: A CE560XL, departing LAS via the COWBY RNAV SID suffered a CFTT incident when ATC deleted the crossing restrictions at ROPPR and the pilot flying flying failed to insure adequate thrust settings to continue the climb after the pilot not flying deleted the crossings from the FMS. rewrite: A CE560XL departing LAS via the COWBY RNAV SID experienced a CFTT incident when ATC removed crossing restrictions at ROPPR. The pilot flying failed to maintain adequate thrust settings after the pilot not flying deleted the crossings from the FMS. A low altitude alert from ATC re-energized the crew's awareness.

text: B777 flight crew describes the circumstances leading up to a go-around during vectors for an ILS to Runway 19L at IAD. A descent is initiated and airspeed gets low due to minimal spacing with the traffic ahead.
rewrite: A B777 flight crew initiated a descent during vectors for an ILS approach to Runway 19L at IAD. Airspeed decreased due to minimal spacing with traffic ahead. The crew prepared for a go-around as the aircraft approached the TOP OF DESCENT.

text: TRACON Controller described a loss of separation event involving two successive arrival aircraft on visual approaches. The reporter listed a new 'video map' that may have been a contributing factor.
rewrite: A TRACON controller reported a loss of separation between two successive arrival aircraft on visual approaches. The incident involved a new 'video map' potentially contributing to the event. The controller noted the aircraft were on visual approaches with no radio communication.

text: A pilot and instructor were in the flare for landing when they spotted another aircraft on approach to the opposite direction runway. They took evasive action and the other aircraft landed normally. They also landed normally after a circuit around the pattern.
rewrite: During the flare for landing, the pilot and instructor observed an aircraft approaching the opposite direction runway. They executed evasive action, allowing the other aircraft to land normally. After completing a circuit around the traffic pattern, they also landed without incident.

text: C-172 instructor and student pilot flying an aircraft with known fuel gauge problems, landed off-field near their destination due to fuel starvation. Although the fuel quantity was visually confirmed prior to departure, the aircraft flew approximately one hour less than standard burn rate would predict.
rewrite: C-172 instructor and student pilot experienced fuel starvation, forcing an off-field landing near their destination. Despite visual confirmation of fuel quantity before departure, the aircraft consumed fuel at a rate approximately one hour less than standard. The fuel gauge issues contributed to the unexpected fuel depletion.

text: Air Carrier reporter claims 127.95 utilized by Maiquetia is unusable for ATC in some locations due to a loud 'squeal' preventing communications.
rewrite: An Air Carrier reporter states that the 127.95 MHz frequency used by Maiquetia is ineffective for ATC in certain areas due to a persistent 'squeal' interfering with communications. The issue affects ATC's ability to maintain clear contact with aircraft. The problem is attributed to a loud noise on the frequency, hindering effective communication.

text: Grumman AA5 pilot experienced a total loss of all onboard avionics electrical power while in IMC when avionics master switch failed. A battery powered Garmin 496 and hand held transceiver were used to land safely. Reporter asserts that this switch, a Toggle Thermal Circuit Breaker, which, upon tripping, cannot be reset by the pilot may violate FAR 23.1357 (d).
rewrite: A Grumman AA5 pilot experienced a total loss of all onboard avionics electrical power during IMC due to failure of the avionics master switch. The pilot utilized a battery-powered Garmin 496 and a handheld transceiver to execute a safe landing. The reporter claims the toggle thermal circuit breaker, which cannot be reset by the pilot upon tripping, may violate FAR 23.1357(d).

text: A King Air flight crew, departing the terminal ramp for Runway 32 at EAU, was confused by taxiway signs to assist him in doing so safely. The confusion was increased by a 'restricted' sign at the end of the ramp from which it was reasonable to expect a taxiway to the runway.
rewrite: A King Air flight crew, departing the terminal ramp for Runway 32 at EAU, encountered confusion while taxiing due to unclear signage. The crew was uncertain of the correct taxiway route to Runway 32. A 'restricted' sign at the end of the ramp further complicated their decision-making process.

text: A B767-300ER flight crew suffered a tail skid strike on a firm landing conducted from a visual approach. The reporters cited the loss of sequential low altitude/flare RA altitude callouts due to the GPWS being deferred was a critical factor.
rewrite: A B767-300ER flight crew experienced a tail skid strike during a firm landing from a visual approach. The loss of sequential low altitude and flare RA altitude callouts, attributed to deferred GPWS activation, was identified as a critical factor in the incident. The crew failed to maintain proper altitude awareness during the landing phase.

text: B777 flight crew experiences a stuck mic during approach to SBGR with the Captain flying and performing communication duties while the First Officer sorts out the mic problem. Vectors to the ILS 27L are received and a descent to 3,900 FT is initiated with the First Officer out of the loop. A terrain warning is annunciated and a go-around initiated after some hesitation.
rewrite: A B777 flight crew encountered a stuck microphone during the approach to SBGR with the Captain handling communication while the First Officer addressed the issue. Vectors to ILS 27L were issued, and a descent to 3,900 FT began with the First Officer not participating. A terrain warning activated, leading to a hesitant go-around initiation.

text: A319 Flight Attendant reported several passengers and crewmembers felt ill from poor cabin air quality.
rewrite: A flight attendant on an A319 reported multiple passengers and crewmembers experiencing illness due to poor cabin air quality. The crew noted unusual symptoms, including dizziness and nausea, prompting an immediate assessment of the aircraft's environmental control system. No specific cause was identified, but the situation was escalated for further investigation.
context: BRAKING ACTION (GOOD, GOOD TO MEDIUM, MEDIUM, MEDIUM TO POOR, POOR, OR NIL)

text: SA227 Captain reported he had directional control difficulties after landing, resulting in two blown tires, runway excursion, and contact with a runway light.
rewrite: SA227 Captain reported directional control issues post-landing, causing two tire blowouts, a runway excursion, and contact with a runway light. The aircraft veered off the runway, impacting the runway entrance lights. The incident occurred during the landing roll, leading to a loss of control and subsequent damage.

text: B747 flight crew describes the circumstances that led up to the entry of incorrect V speeds into the FMC. The ZFW of 498k was used instead of the actual TOGW of 853K for the V speed calculation. The Captain detects the anomaly during the takeoff roll and delays rotation until closer to the actual V2 speed of 180 knots.
rewrite: During takeoff roll, the B747 crew noticed an incorrect V speed calculation in the FMC, caused by using ZFW of 498k instead of the actual TOGW of 853k. The Captain detected the anomaly and delayed rotation to align with the correct V2 speed of 180 knots. The error affected the V speeds entered into the FMC.

text: An ERJ-145 flight crew initiated an emergency descent, declared an emergency with ATC and, ulimately, returned to their departure airport following the loss of both air conditioning and pressurization packs.
rewrite: An ERJ-145 flight crew initiated an emergency descent, declared an emergency with ATC, and ultimately returned to their departure airport after experiencing a loss of both air conditioning and pressurization packs. The crew lost both packs, leading to a loss of pressurization, and initiated a descent to maintain cabin pressure. The flight followed a round robin flight plan to return to the departure airport.

text: A Line Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reports about a Part Power Stop (PPS) that was inadvertently engaged on a B757-200 aircraft engine after a Fuel Flow Governor replacement. Technician also noted the lack of a positive lockout mechanism to properly secure the PPS.
rewrite: A Line Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reported an inadvertent engagement of the Part Power Stop (PPS) on a B757-200 engine following a Fuel Flow Governor replacement. The technician noted the absence of a positive lockout mechanism to secure the PPS, raising concerns about potential safety risks during engine operation.

text: MD-11 flight crew reports rejecting a takeoff at 110 KTS for a number three engine fire warning. The aircraft had a history of false and incomplete fire warnings. Autobrakes did not disengage with manual braking as expected requiring autobrake switch to be selected off, which contributed to hot brakes.
rewrite: An MD-11 flight crew rejected takeoff at 110 KTS due to a number three engine fire warning. The crew had a history of false and incomplete fire warnings. Autobrakes failed to disengage, requiring manual braking and activation of the autobrake switch, resulting in hot brakes.
context: BRAKING ACTION (GOOD, GOOD TO MEDIUM, MEDIUM, MEDIUM TO POOR, POOR, OR NIL)

text: B747 Captain experiences the failure of the number one hydraulic system in cruise due to loss of hydraulic fluid and the confusion that reigns while trying to interpret the QRH procedure for this failure. Eventually it is determined that the aircraft can continue to destination.
rewrite: During cruise, a B747 Captain encountered a failure of the number one hydraulic system due to loss of hydraulic fluid. Confusion arose as the crew attempted to interpret the QRH procedure. After assessing the situation, it was determined the aircraft could safely continue to its destination.

text: IFR inbound to OAK elected to climb above the ATC assigned altitude to the published MEA when experiencing communications problems, the reporter noting MVA's should be available to pilots for safety clarity.
rewrite: IFR inbound to OAK, pilot elected to climb above ATC assigned altitude to published MEA due to communications issues. Reporter noted MVA should be available for safety and clarity. Pilot exercised pilot’s discretion to manage climb rate and timing.

text: G-200 Captain reported on takeoff from 36U he had not properly briefed the second segment climb requirements and got a GPWS TERRAIN alert.
rewrite: G-200 Captain reported on takeoff from 36U that he had not properly briefed the second segment climb requirements, resulting in a GPWS TERRAIN alert during climbout. The alert indicated potential terrain proximity, prompting immediate pilot action. The captain acknowledged the warning and initiated corrective measures to ensure safe altitude maintenance.
context: IFR TAKEOFF MINIMUMS AND DEPARTURE PROCEDURES

text: B737 Captain reported he got an internal wind shear alert on takeoff roll that he chose to ignore because conditions did not seem conducive to windshear, but after takeoff he heard the Tower issue a similar alert to an inbound flight.
rewrite: A B737 captain reported an internal wind shear alert during takeoff roll, which he disregarded as conditions appeared unfavorable. He later learned the tower had issued a similar alert to an inbound flight, prompting concern about potential wind shear in the terminal environment. The alert was triggered by the predictive wind shear alert system (PWS) monitoring the approach path.

text: Air Carrier Captain reports an overly loud RAAS warning requiring the crew to ask the Tower to repeat the last transmission.
rewrite: An air carrier captain reports an overly loud RAAS warning, prompting the crew to request the tower to repeat the last transmission. The crew says "Say again all after ABRAM VOR" to clarify the previous communication. The tower acknowledges the request and repeats the transmission.

text: B737-800 Captain departing Runway 14L at ORD reports a conflict with an Airbus landing Runway 22R. The Airbus is sent around by the Tower.
rewrite: A B737-800 Captain departing Runway 14L at ORD reported a conflict with an Airbus A380 landing on Runway 22R. The Airbus was vectored around by Tower to avoid the conflict. The situation occurred during departure roll.

text: After arriving at Runway 13 for takeoff, a CRJ200 Captain is advised that his departure gate is closed due to weather and to taxi onto Runway 13 and exit at AA. The crew cannot find the taxiway due to poor lighting and a lack of signs, requiring some assistance from ATC.
rewrite: After arriving at Runway 13 for takeoff, the CRJ200 Captain was advised to taxi onto Runway 13 and exit at AA due to a closed departure gate. The crew struggled to locate the taxiway amid poor lighting and missing signs, prompting them to request assistance from ATC.

text: An experienced pilot was distracted by conversation with a passenger and neglected to remove the tow bar during pre-flight. This was discovered when attempting to reposition into the hangar after the flight. The tow bar was found off the runway with no damage to the aircraft.
rewrite: An experienced pilot became distracted during pre-flight conversation with a passenger and failed to remove the tow bar. The oversight was identified later when attempting to reposition the aircraft into the hangar. The tow bar was found off the runway, and the aircraft sustained no damage.

text: B757-200 flight crew described operational complications arising from flying the aircraft with multiple MELs.
rewrite: A B757-200 flight crew encountered operational challenges while flying with multiple MEL items in effect, impacting system performance and required procedures during various flight phases. The MELs affected avionics, hydraulics, and engine systems, necessitating alternate checklists and monitoring of critical flight parameters. Crew coordination was essential to ensure compliance with MEL requirements and maintain safe aircraft operation.

text: An EMB-145 flight crew suffered a main pitch trim failure. The completed the QRH procedure and determined they could continue to destination using the autopilot which they disconnected from time to time to allow manual retrimming.
rewrite: An EMB-145 flight crew experienced a main pitch trim failure during cruise. They completed the QRH procedure and decided to continue to destination using the autopilot, disengaging it periodically to manually retrim the aircraft.

text: C170 Instructor reports a ground loop by the pilot flying during a touch and go. The instructor takes control but is unable to prevent the left wing tip and horizontal stabilizer from contacting the ground.
rewrite: During a touch-and-go maneuver, the pilot flying experienced a ground loop. The instructor took control but could not prevent the left wing tip and horizontal stabilizer from contacting the ground. The incident occurred during the landing phase of the training exercise.

text: A B737-300 flight crew returned to their departure airport after suffering the failure the IRS.
rewrite: A B737-300 flight crew executed a ROUND flight plan, returning to their departure airport after experiencing a failure in the Inertial Reference System (IRS). The crew initiated a diversion procedure due to the loss of navigation accuracy, resulting in an unscheduled return to the original departure airport. The incident occurred during the en route phase of the flight.

text: Tower Controller described a momentary loss of MVA separation when an air carrier departure experienced a bird strike, entered a wide downwind, and returned to the airport.
rewrite: The tower controller noted a temporary loss of MVA separation as a departing air carrier aircraft encountered a bird strike, entered a wide downwind pattern, and returned to the airport without establishing contact with the control tower. The nonapproach control tower was responsible for sequencing the aircraft in the traffic pattern and ensuring separation. The incident occurred during the departure phase of a round-robin flight plan.

text: A BAE-125-850XP at FL230 crew declared an emergency, began a descent to 10,000 FT and completed the checklist as the cabin altitude climbed but later continued to the destination at 12,000 FT. Maintenance had not previously secured an air conditioning duct.
rewrite: A BAE-125-850XP crew at FL230 declared an emergency, initiated a descent to 10,000 FT, and completed the checklist as cabin altitude increased. Despite the emergency, the aircraft continued to the destination at 12,000 FT. Maintenance had not secured an air conditioning duct prior to the flight.

text: PA28 pilot reports a runway excursion during takeoff when the pilot seat slides back, causing damage to the aircraft and a runway light.
rewrite: A PA28 pilot experienced a runway excursion during takeoff when the pilot seat slid back, resulting in aircraft damage and activation of a runway light. The incident occurred during the takeoff roll, with the pilot reporting the seat movement and subsequent loss of control. The runway light indicated an unsafe condition for departure, prompting the pilot to stop the takeoff.

text: TRACON Controller described an apparent loss of separation by an adjacent facility, the adjacent facility claiming diverging courses was applied.
rewrite: The TRACON controller reported a potential loss of separation involving an adjacent facility. The adjacent facility stated they had applied diverging courses to maintain separation. The situation involved coordinated procedures between the two facilities.

text: PA28 pilot reports being unable to obtain fuel at a planned fuel stop and electing to continue VFR over approaching frontal weather. Class A airspace is entered avoiding clouds which are noticed by ATC. ATC provides assistance to the private pilot to descend in IMC to 5,000 FT for a visual approach at a suitable airport.
rewrite: A PA28 pilot was unable to obtain fuel at a planned stop and elected to continue VFR over approaching frontal weather. While entering Class A airspace, the pilot avoided clouds, which were noticed by ATC. ATC assisted the private pilot to descend into IMC to 5,000 FT for a visual approach at a suitable airport.

text: A flight crew discovered enroute that all ZAN approach and airport charts were removed from their respective flight kits even though preflight checks indicated both kits onboard were current.
rewrite: During enroute flight, the crew discovered that all ZAN approach and airport charts were missing from both flight kits, despite preflight checks confirming the kits were current. The absence of these essential navigation documents posed a risk to continued operations. The crew had to rely on onboard navigation systems and communicate with ATC for guidance.

text: Shortly after takeoff the pilot of a Diamond DA40 lost situational awareness when his iPad shut down and his G1000 appeared to be malfunctioning. Realizing that he was off course when his first intended waypoint loomed off the left wing, he became concerned that he may have violated Class B airspace.
rewrite: Shortly after takeoff, the pilot of a Diamond DA40 lost situational awareness when his iPad shut down and the G1000 appeared to malfunction. Realizing he was off course as the first intended waypoint approached from the left, he became concerned about potentially entering Class B airspace.

text: B777 Captain reports the inability to access iPad information due to the lack of a keypad to enter the security code after a recent IOS upgrade.
rewrite: A B777 captain reported being unable to access iPad information following an iOS upgrade, as the device lacked a keypad for entering a security code. The pilot indicated the issue prevented secure access to necessary flight data. The captain requested assistance in resolving the security code entry problem.

text: A pilot in a King Air was distracted during a maintenance flight with a mechanic, and neglected to activate the auto ignition switches. When he noticed, he reached for the switches but unintentionally activated the starter generators, removing generator power from the electrical system. After a successful return to the departure airport, he discovered that his radio was unable to contact Ground Control, likely due to the exhaustion of the battery power.
rewrite: A pilot operating a King Air on a maintenance flight with a mechanic was distracted and failed to activate the auto ignition switches. Upon realizing the oversight, he reached for the switches but inadvertently engaged the starter generators, depleting the electrical system's generator power. After returning to the departure airport, he found his radio unable to contact Ground Control, likely due to battery power exhaustion.

text: An MD-80 arriving at its destination with minimum fuel was directed to go-around due to an airport emergency. They declared a fuel emergency and received appropriate special handling, arriving at the gate with fuel remaining of 2,700 LBS.
rewrite: An MD-80 approaching the destination with minimum fuel was instructed to go-around due to an airport emergency. The crew declared a fuel emergency, prompting special handling. Upon arrival, they reported fuel remaining of 2,700 pounds.

text: An ASH-25 Glider's aft cockpit left rudder cable became disconnected during flight, but the aircraft was fully controllable from the front cockpit.
rewrite: An ASH-25 glider experienced a disconnection of the aft cockpit left rudder cable during flight, yet the aircraft remained fully controllable from the front cockpit. The incident occurred during the cruise phase, with no immediate loss of control or adverse effects on flight safety. The pilot maintained control using the front cockpit controls throughout the event.

text: An Air Carrier First Officer flying a night visual to MCO Runway 18R descended below the ORL 2,500 FT crossing restricting but corrected after the Captain's alert. The Captain reported new Company procedures take one pilot out of the loop during this period of the arrival.
rewrite: An Air Carrier First Officer conducting a night visual approach to MCO Runway 18R descended below the ORL 2,500 FT crossing restriction. The Captain alerted the First Officer, who then corrected the descent. The Captain noted new company procedures involve one pilot being out of the loop during this arrival phase.

text: B737 Captain in a holding pattern, is requested by Dispatch to hold as long as possible and plan on arriving at the nearby alternate with 4,000 LBS of fuel. The alternate is also IMC and this plan is rejected. Holding is departed to land at the alternate with 6,000 LBS.
rewrite: A B737 captain was holding in a holding pattern, requested by Dispatch to hold as long as possible to arrive at a nearby alternate with 4,000 lbs of fuel. The alternate was also in IMC, and the plan was rejected. The captain departed the hold to land at the alternate with 6,000 lbs of fuel remaining.

text: BE1900 Captain experiences a propeller malfunction requiring an in flight shutdown. An emergency is declared and flight lands safely at destination.
rewrite: BE1900 captain reported a propeller malfunction, necessitating an in-flight shutdown. The crew declared an emergency and diverted to the destination airport for a safe landing. The propeller was feathered to minimize drag and engine rotation.

text: A late runway change clearance as the airliner was only a few miles from the runway transition IF resulted in a temporary track deviation as the flight crew attempted to program the change. ATC provided vectors for the subsequent approach.
rewrite: A late runway change clearance as the airliner was only a few miles from the runway transition IF resulted in a temporary track deviation as the flight crew attempted to program the change. ATC provided vectors for the subsequent approach. The crew reported a 5-mile final for Runway 22.

text: A80 Controller described a loss of separation event by the ZTL Controller when he/she allowed a climbing and descending aircraft to pass within two miles, the reporter indicating training intervention should have been initiated.
rewrite: The ZTL Controller failed to maintain separation by allowing a climbing and descending aircraft to pass within two miles. The controller described this as a loss of separation event. The reporter suggests training intervention should have been initiated to prevent such occurrences.

text: A MD-82 Captain dispatched with wing tank fuel only because of center tank pump MEL, decided to bypass a fuel stop and upon arrival at the final destination declared minimum fuel then rejected the Tower's go-around command with traffic exiting the runway.
rewrite: An MD-82 captain, operating with wing tank fuel only due to a center tank pump MEL, bypassed a scheduled fuel stop. Upon arrival, the crew declared minimum fuel. The pilot then rejected the tower's go-around command as traffic exited the runway.

text: A Flight Attendant notified that Captain that a stray life vest was found in a compartment, and that the vest was out of date. When Maintenance personnel identified the location of the missing vest, they also discovered that many more life vests were out of date. The Captain was concerned about the maintenance procedures that allowed this to occur as well as the security inspections that did not uncover the discrepancy.
rewrite: A flight attendant informed the captain of a stray life vest found in a compartment, which was found to be expired. Maintenance personnel, while locating the missing vest, discovered multiple additional life vests were also expired. The captain expressed concern over maintenance procedures and security inspections that failed to detect the issue.

text: Air Carrier Captain reports entering severe turbulence and windshear at 4,000 FT with airspeeds of plus and minus 45 KTS and bank angles to 30 degrees. Inability to read flight instruments accurately due to turbulence also reported.
rewrite: Air Carrier Captain encountered severe turbulence and windshear at 4,000 FT, experiencing airspeed variations of ±45 KTS and bank angles up to 30 degrees. Turbulence affected instrument readability, making accurate readings difficult. Pilots reported the turbulence as severe due to significant aircraft reaction.

text: B777 flight crew reports descending below their assigned altitude due to the altimeter setting being changed by the flying First Officer from QNE to QNH just as the aircraft is leveling at 6,000 FT. The aircraft levels off 300 FT low on QNH and is immediately returned to 6,000 FT.
rewrite: The B777 flight crew descended below their assigned altitude when the First Officer changed the altimeter setting from QNE to QNH as the aircraft was leveling off at 6,000 FT. The aircraft leveled off 300 FT low on QNH and was immediately returned to 6,000 FT. The crew reported the discrepancy due to the altimeter setting change.

text: C182 pilot reports departing on a short (20 NM) night flight and experiencing electrical problems. The flight is continued ducking under low clouds until arriving directly over the airport at 1,000 AGL with no lights or radio.
rewrite: A C182 pilot departed on a short night flight, encountering electrical issues. The pilot continued the flight by ducking under low clouds, maintaining 1,000 AGL until arriving directly over the airport with no lights or radio operational. The flight was conducted without ATC contact or visual references.

text: A pilot took off for a short flight from VPZ Runway 27 which was NOTAMed closed, but he had not checked NOTAMs and noted he monitored ASOS which the airport was prohibited from using as an airport status notification tool.
rewrite: A pilot departed from VPZ Runway 27, which was NOTAMed closed, but he did not check NOTAMs. He relied on ASOS for airport status, though the airport prohibited its use as a notification tool. The runway was closed by airport management, and the pilot failed to verify the closure before takeoff.

text: DAL Controller described a runway incursion event involving an aircraft taxiing to Runway 13L, the reporter claimed multiple same type occurrences and the existing hold lines are problematic and need adjusting.
rewrite: A Dallas controller reported a runway incursion where an aircraft taxiing to Runway 13L failed to clear the hold line, prompting a safety concern. The reporter noted multiple similar incidents, citing issues with existing hold lines. Adjustments to the hold lines are recommended to prevent future occurrences.

text: MD-83 flight crew reported left engine loss of power shortly after takeoff, the result of a probable compressor stall. Flight declared an emergency and returned to departure airport with affected engine at idle thrust.
rewrite: MD-83 flight crew experienced a loss of power in the left engine shortly after takeoff, likely due to a compressor stall. The crew declared an emergency and initiated a return to the departure airport with the affected engine at idle thrust. The situation did not involve a flameout or critical engine failure.

text: A319 flight crew reported they were notified by a Flight Attendant that a passenger had pointed out missing skin in the area of Number 2 Engine. Flight declared an emergency and returned to departure airport, where postflight inspection revealed the Number 2 Engine cowl had departed the aircraft in flight.
rewrite: A319 flight crew received a report from a flight attendant that a passenger noticed missing skin on the Number 2 Engine. The crew declared an emergency and diverted back to the departure airport. Post-flight inspection confirmed the Number 2 Engine cowl had separated from the aircraft during flight.

text: The instructor pilot in Beech Texan II was distracted looking for the airport as the student failed to arrest their descent at the MDA. ATC issued an altitude alert and they recovered back to the MDA.
rewrite: The instructor pilot in a Beech Texan II was distracted searching for the airport while the student failed to arrest descent at the Minimum Descent Altitude (MDA). ATC issued an altitude alert, prompting the crew to recover back to the MDA. The pilot then continued the approach.

text: Tower Controller described a required go-around event when he/she failed to properly scan for arrivals before issuing a takeoff clearance with traffic on short final.
rewrite: The tower controller issued a takeoff clearance without properly scanning for arrivals, resulting in a required go-around due to traffic on short final. The controller failed to detect an arriving aircraft within the arrival/departure window, leading to a conflict. This oversight compromised safety during the departure phase.

text: B737 First Officer laments his company's new fuel policy that is exacerbated by flight plans with unrealistic altitude assumptions, resulting in low arrival fuel.
rewrite: A B737 First Officer expresses frustration with the airline's new fuel policy, which, combined with flight plans based on unrealistic altitude assumptions, leads to insufficient arrival fuel. The policy results in low fuel remaining upon arrival, prompting the pilot to note the approximate number of minutes of fuel left. The issue stems from operational inefficiencies in fuel planning and altitude selection.

text: Air Carrier First Officer reports that all the fixes necessary to fly the ILS36R at CLT do not load unless the HEKAM transition is selected when loading the ILS. Crew crosses HEKAM at 4,000 FT per ATC and starts descent to 3,000 FT not realising that two more fixes need to be crossed at 4,000 FT before descent is commenced. Glideslope was out of service.
rewrite: The First Officer reported that all fixes for the ILS36R at CLT do not load unless the HEKAM transition is selected. The crew crossed HEKAM at 4,000 FT as instructed and initiated descent to 3,000 FT without realizing two additional fixes required crossing at 4,000 FT. The glideslope was inoperative.

text: The First Officer aboard a CE-680 repeatedly reminded his Captain to maintain their assigned altitude as the Captain appeared uncertain of the autopilot vertical navigation functions. Several modest deviations were initiated and arrested without comment from ATC.
rewrite: The First Officer on CE-680 repeatedly reminded the Captain to maintain the last assigned altitude as the Captain was unsure of the autopilot's VNAV functions. The Captain made several minor altitude deviations, which were corrected without ATC intervention. The crew remained in communication with ATC throughout the event.

text: An instructor in the LAL Runway 5 closed traffic pattern took evasive action during a near miss with a light twin which departed Runway 9.
rewrite: An instructor conducting a straight-in approach VFR into Runway 5 encountered a light twin departing Runway 9, prompting evasive action to avoid a near miss during closed runway traffic. The instructor's maneuver was necessary due to the conflicting traffic patterns and unsafe proximity between the two aircraft.

text: A B737-800 Captain and First Officer discovered their oxygen mask pressures at 0 PSI during the preflight mask test and maintenance discovered the oxygen bottle valve not fully open after the bottle had been replaced the previous night.
rewrite: During the preflight mask test, the B737-800 Captain and First Officer noted both oxygen mask pressures at 0 PSI. Maintenance later found the oxygen bottle valve was not fully open after the bottle had been replaced the previous night. The issue was traced to the valve not being fully opened during the replacement.

text: A pilot at CTAF IWS believed the next arrival aircraft was on base but after getting into position and holding for the previous arrival to clear the runway, another unseen aircraft executed a go-around over him.
rewrite: A pilot at CTAF IWS believed the next arrival aircraft was on base. After positioning and holding short for the previous arrival to clear the runway, an unseen aircraft executed a go-around overhead. The pilot was unaware of the aircraft's presence until it initiated the maneuver.

text: When the ERJ-170 flight crew inadvertently utilized the wrong checklist in response to an EICAS Air Data System message received just prior to takeoff they believed they had corrected the problem. After maintenance action taken at their destination they realized their error.
rewrite: During the pre-takeoff phase, the ERJ-170 flight crew mistakenly used an incorrect checklist in response to an EICAS Air Data System message, believing they had resolved the issue. Later, after maintenance was performed at their destination, the crew recognized their error and initiated corrective action.

text: A B737-700 FUEL MASTER CAUTION alerted when the right tank fuel quantity decreased more quickly than the left tank and after completing the Fuel Leak Checklist the crew shutdown the right engine, declared an emergency and returned to the departure airport. A faulty crossfeed valve was suspected.
rewrite: A B737-700 triggered a FUEL MASTER CAUTION as the right tank fuel quantity decreased faster than the left. After completing the Fuel Leak Checklist, the crew shut down the right engine, declared an emergency, and diverted back to the departure airport. A faulty crossfeed valve was suspected.

text: Taxiing CRJ900 flight crew was alerted to frost on the starboard winglet by personnel in de-ice truck. First Officer had overlooked the winglet on walk-around.
rewrite: During taxiing, the CRJ900 flight crew was alerted to frost on the starboard winglet by de-ice truck personnel. The First Officer had overlooked the winglet during the pre-flight walk-around.

text: MD11 flight crew is informed by the Tower during landing roll that fluid was observed streaming from the left engine during approach and continues. The left engine is shut down with no change in the fluid flow. All engines are shut down and the aircraft is towed to the gate.
rewrite: During the landing roll, Tower advised MD11 crew of fluid streaming from the left engine. The crew shut down the left engine, but fluid flow continued. All engines were subsequently shut down, and the aircraft was towed to the gate.

text: While a Maintenance Technician was starting an engine, a ground support vehicle drove through the restricted box in front of the aircraft.
rewrite: During engine start by a Maintenance Technician, a ground support vehicle entered the restricted area in front of the aircraft, violating established safety protocols. The vehicle's movement occurred while the engine was being started, posing a potential hazard to the maintenance operation. No prior warning or clearance was given for the vehicle's entry into the restricted box.

text: A CL30 Captain railed against the intrusive nature of RAAS warnings when taxiing on busy airports. Believes flight crew control of warning volume is an acceptable alternative.
rewrite: A CL30 Captain expressed frustration with the intrusive RAAS warnings during taxi operations at a busy airport. The pilot suggested that allowing flight crew to control warning volume would be a more acceptable alternative. The concern centered on the disruptive nature of automated alerts during ground movements.
context: EN ROUTE MINIMUM SAFE ALTITUDE WARNING (E

text: When they took off from TEB with the pitch trim switch in the secondary vice primary position the pilot flying was unable to maintain the required 1,500 MSL level off on the RUUDY SID. After repositioning the switch operation returned to normal.
rewrite: During the takeoff from TEB, the pilot flying was unable to maintain the required 1,500 MSL level off on the RUUDY SID with the pitch trim switch in the secondary position. Repositioning the switch restored normal operations.

text: A Maintenance Manager was informed he had installed four incorrect replacement bolts at the lower Eyelet Fitting for the cockpit windshield center-post to the forward fuselage on an EMB-145 aircraft. He had verified the Part Number (P/N) on a certification sheet had matched the Engineering Order (E/O), but was unaware that the bolts that were issued did not match the certification.
rewrite: The Maintenance Manager installed four incorrect replacement bolts at the lower Eyelet Fitting on the EMB-145 cockpit windshield center-post to the forward fuselage. The error occurred during maintenance without proper verification of the actual components.

text: Captain reports he had three separate and sequential incidences of Number 2 Engine flaming out in cruise that required single engine approaches in the same Piper PA-42 aircraft. All three inflight engine failures were due to the Main Fuel High Pressure stainless steel line breaking near the Fuel Control Unit (FCU) on the same PT 6A-41 engine.
rewrite: Captain reported three sequential Number 2 engine flameouts during cruise in a Piper PA-42, necessitating single-engine approaches. Each failure was caused by the Main Fuel High Pressure stainless steel line breaking near the Fuel Control Unit (FCU) on the PT 6A-41 engine. All incidents involved the critical engine, requiring feathered propeller and flameout pattern procedures.

text: SLC Tower cleared a B737 for takeoff while the aircraft ahead was still on the runway. Then as the B737 accelerated beyond 70 KTS, the following aircraft was cleared for takeoff. An abort would have caused a serious problem.
rewrite: SLC Tower cleared a B737 for takeoff while the preceding aircraft was still on the runway. As the B737 accelerated beyond 70 KTS, the following aircraft was cleared for takeoff. An abort at this point would have resulted in a serious conflict due to insufficient accelerate-stop distance available.

text: A MD-83 taxied into a confined gate area at night with Marshalers present, but the wingtip still contacted a fuel truck in close proximity to the gate.
rewrite: An MD-83 taxiing into a confined gate area at night encountered a fuel truck near the gate, despite marshals being present. The wingtip struck the truck, causing damage. The incident occurred during the ground phase of the flight.

text: B737 Captain reports having to stop abruptly approaching the gate to avoid a tug pulling carts that suddenly cuts in front of the aircraft.
rewrite: A B737 captain reported an abrupt stop while approaching the approach gate to avoid a tug pulling carts that unexpectedly cut in front of the aircraft. The pilot had to apply full braking to prevent a collision. The incident occurred during the final approach phase, just short of the approach gate.

text: A Piper 140 pilot encountered violent rotor wash from military helicopters maneuvering in close proximity to the active runway.
rewrite: A Piper 140 pilot reported encountering violent rotor wash from military helicopters operating in close proximity to the active runway during takeoff. The helicopters were maneuvering near the runway, creating significant downwash that affected the Piper 140's performance. The pilot noted the turbulence was severe and impacted aircraft control.

text: Air carrier flight crew reported descending early on the VOR DME 31 to AMA, when the CF31 fix is confused with the FF31. The error is detected at about the same time ATC issues a low altitude alert. DME was not used to define the waypoints.
rewrite: Air carrier flight crew descended early on the VOR DME 31 to AMA, confusing the CF31 fix with FF31. The error was detected simultaneously with an ATC low altitude alert. DME was not used to define the waypoints, leading to navigational confusion.

text: A First Officer and Maintenance Controller report how a left engine thrust reverser MEL deferral was inadvertently applied to a CRJ-200 aircraft that already had the left engine cowl anti-ice pressure relief valve deferred. Contributing factor was the lack of any cross-reference information in the thrust reverser MEL section that deferral of both items on the same side of aircraft, was not allowed.
rewrite: A First Officer and Maintenance Controller reported an inadvertent application of a left engine thrust reverser MEL deferral to a CRJ-200 aircraft already with the left engine cowl anti-ice pressure relief valve deferred. The issue stemmed from the absence of cross-reference information in the thrust reverser MEL section, which failed to note that deferral of both items on the same side was not allowed. This led to a potential safety risk due to the critical engine being affected.

text: DHC-300 flight crew experiences fluctuating torque on the number one engine at rotation that quickly increases in amplitude until auto feather is triggered. An emergency is declared and flight returns to the departure airport. This engine had a history of similar incidents.
rewrite: During rotation, the DHC-300 flight crew encountered fluctuating torque on the number one engine, which rapidly increased in amplitude, prompting an auto feather. The crew declared an emergency and diverted back to the departure airport. The engine had a history of similar incidents.

text: PA32 pilot reports pilot submitting the required international flight plan and eApis form in a timely manner prior to flight. The pilot believed that because it was VFR conditions at the time of flight, the flight could take place under VFR rules and that there was no requirement to talk to ATC and obtain a unique squawk code.
rewrite: A PA32 pilot submitted the required international flight plan and eAPIS form on time. The pilot believed VFR conditions allowed flight under VFR rules, assuming no need to contact ATC or obtain a unique squawk code. The pilot was unaware of the requirement for an abbreviated IFR flight plan under VFR not recommended conditions.

text: A Contract Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reports about the constant problem of having to request Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) and General Manual (GM) hard copies prior to performing maintenance actions on an Air Carrier's aircraft.
rewrite: A Contract Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) frequently encounters the need to request Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) and General Manual (GM) hard copies before conducting maintenance actions on an Air Carrier's aircraft, leading to delays and inefficiencies in the maintenance process. The AMT notes that digital access to these manuals is limited, necessitating repeated requests for physical copies. This issue persists despite the availability of digital resources, causing operational friction in maintenance planning.

text: An EMB-145 Captain noted that, although they had been accumulating rime ice on the windshield the icing valves had not automatically opened. When he opened them manually the EICAS opined 'Anti-ice On/No Icing.'
rewrite: An EMB-145 captain reported accumulating rime ice on the windshield despite icing valves not automatically opening. Upon manual activation, the EICAS displayed 'Anti-ice On/No Icing,' indicating the system did not detect icing conditions. The pilot confirmed the presence of rime ice, suggesting a discrepancy between actual conditions and system response.

text: A B737 took evasive action from a RJ taxiing at a very high speed which ORD Ground Control and Tower were not coordinating with other traffic.
rewrite: A B737 took evasive action to avoid a RJ taxiing at high speed. ORD Ground Control and Tower failed to coordinate with other traffic, leading to the incident. The situation involved uncoordinated taxi movements during ground operations.

text: CRJ-200 First Officer describes a near loss of control incident shortly after takeoff with the Captain flying in moderate turbulence. A rudder anomaly was thought to be the issue and a large amount of left rudder trim was required to bring the aircraft back to stable flight.
rewrite: During takeoff, the CRJ-200 encountered moderate turbulence, leading to a near loss of control. The Captain reported a rudder anomaly, requiring significant left rudder trim to stabilize the aircraft. The First Officer noted the issue and assisted in restoring control.

text: SMA pilot at a CTAF airport holding off the runway, witnessed another small aircraft land long on a short runway then experienced a runway excursion.
rewrite: SMA pilot at a CTAF airport held off the runway, observed another small aircraft land long on a short runway, resulting in a runway excursion. The pilot noted the aircraft exceeded the available landing distance, leading to an overrun. The incident occurred during the landing phase, with no prior LAHSO instructions issued.

text: Pilot of a single engine, fixed gear aircraft in IMC requested and was cleared for a GPS approach to destination airport only to find that the GPS approach to that airport was not in his Garmin GPS. Pilot maneuvered to VMC and landed. Pilot later acertained that Garmin 'excludes' certain approaches from their database and pilots must therefore check a Garmin website for 'excluded approaches.'
rewrite: Pilot of a single-engine, fixed-gear aircraft in IMC requested and was cleared for a GPS approach to the destination airport. However, the GPS approach was not available on the Garmin GPS. The pilot maneuvered to VMC and landed. Subsequently, the pilot learned that Garmin excludes certain approaches from its database, requiring pilots to check the Garmin website for excluded approaches.

text: A pilot departing VHHH noted that the PECAN 1A and OCEAN 2A have 5,000 FT RAMEN and PORPA climb constraints specified in the FMS RNAV procedure, but while a 5,000 FT is a general climb constraint, it does not appear to be associated with waypoints.
rewrite: A pilot departing VHHH reported that PECAN 1A and OCEAN 2A have 5,000 FT RAMEN and PORPA climb constraints in the FMS RNAV procedure. While 5,000 FT is a general climb constraint, it is not linked to specific waypoints. The pilot noted the constraint does not align with the expected procedure.

text: ZMA Controller reports of traffic being funneled over one fix causing an operational error issue to speed differences.
rewrite: ZMA Controller reported traffic being funneled over a single fix, leading to an operational error due to speed differences among aircraft. The error was noted as an Oceanic Error, prompting a report under FAA Order JO 7210.632. Pilots were advised to resume normal speed, but speed restrictions from published procedures remained in effect.

text: B747 flight crew reports an altitude deviation descending into ZSPD due to not converting meters to feet before entering the number into the MCP. Other difficulties operating in the Shanghai FIR and into the ZSPD airport are also discussed.
rewrite: A B747 flight crew reported an altitude deviation while descending into ZSPD due to failing to convert meters to feet before entering the MCP. The crew also discussed operational challenges within the Shanghai FIR and during approach to ZSPD. The error led to a discrepancy between the reported and actual altitude, prompting a STOP ALTITUDE SQUAWK from ATC.

text: CRJ200 First Officer discovers at the top of descent that the number one engine thrust cannot be reduced by pulling back on the thrust lever. The engine is shut down and a single engine landing ensues.
rewrite: At the top of descent, the CRJ200 First Officer noticed the number one engine thrust could not be reduced by pulling the thrust lever. The engine was subsequently shut down, leading to a single-engine landing. The critical engine failure occurred during the approach phase.

text: Controllers at ZHU complain about the responsibility of having to know and provide NOTAM information to pilots after an aircraft is cleared for an instrument approach to a closed runway.
rewrite: Controllers at ZHU express concern over the responsibility of providing NOTAM information to pilots after an aircraft has been cleared for an instrument approach to a closed runway. The issue arises when the approach clearance is issued without proper verification of runway status. This creates a gap in situational awareness and safety protocols.

text: A C182 private pilot departing VGT at night becomes concerned about terrain to the west when the aircraft does not perform as expected and the requested route of flight directly over LAS is not granted.
rewrite: A C182 private pilot departing VGT at night expressed concern about terrain to the west after the aircraft did not perform as expected. The pilot requested a route of flight directly over LAS, but the request was not granted. The pilot was using MULTICOM to communicate with ATC.

text: DAB Controller reports of an computer issue related to STARS. When changing aircraft type, the STARS changes aircraft from VFR to IFR.
rewrite: The DAB controller encountered a computer issue with STARS when switching aircraft types, causing the system to incorrectly change the aircraft status from VFR to IFR. This transition affected the display and tracking of the aircraft within the en route structure. The controller noted the anomaly during a routine update of the aircraft's status.

text: Pilot at LFT airport reports of bad communication procedures at the airport that they thought almost caused them to be part of a runway incursion.
rewrite: Pilot at LFT airport reported poor communication procedures, which they believed nearly led to a runway incursion. The pilot mentioned a hot spot area with potential collision risk. They noted confusion during taxi operations due to unclear radio communications.

text: ZBW describes situation where he is distracted by one aircraft while two others lose required separation.
rewrite: ZBW was distracted by one aircraft when two others lost required separation. The situation occurred during the INCERFA phase, indicating uncertainty about the safety of the aircraft. Increased separation required (ISR) was not maintained, leading to a potential safety risk.

text: Pilot complains about re-route with fixes they are not familiar with and having to enter them to the FMS, while flying close to the first intersection.
rewrite: Pilot reports being rerouted with unfamiliar fixes near the first intersection, requiring manual entry into the FMS while flying close to the COASTAL FIX. The pilot expresses concern over the unexpected route changes and the need to input unfamiliar waypoints during the approach phase.

text: Small aircraft pilot reports that the runways at FMH do not have REIL's and the beginning of the runway is difficult to judge.
rewrite: A small aircraft pilot reported that the runways at FMH lack REILs, making it challenging to determine the beginning of the runway. The pilot noted difficulty in judging the runway's start, which could affect proper positioning for takeoff or landing. The pilot did not mention any specific braking action or displaced threshold conditions.
context: BRAKING ACTION (GOOD, GOOD TO MEDIUM, MEDIUM, MEDIUM TO POOR, POOR, OR NIL)

text: ZME controller reports of problems associated with similar sounding and written intersections. Confusion of aircraft that may or may not be coming into their airspace.
rewrite: ZME controller reports confusion due to similar-sounding and written intersections, leading to uncertainty about aircraft entering their airspace. Pilots and controllers experienced difficulty distinguishing between intersections, increasing the risk of conflict. The situation involved potential misidentification of aircraft positions within the airspace.

text: MD-82 Captain rejected takeoff at 120 KTS due to 10% less N1 and 25 degrees lower EGT on right engine than left engine. EPR's were matched at 2.04. Successful reject with no issues other than required brake cooling.
rewrite: MD-82 Captain rejected takeoff at 120 KTS due to 10% lower N1 and 25 degrees reduced EGT on the right engine compared to the left. Engine pressures were matched at 2.04 EPR. The reject was successful with no other issues except for required brake cooling.

text: ZHU Controller describes scenario where a departure is taken off its route to allow its climb, while it comes into conflict with two arrivals. The Controller describes the routes are not able to climb or descend traffic laterally but controllers do this everyday.
rewrite: ZHU controller coordinated a departure to deviate from its assigned ATS route to initiate climb, resulting in conflict with two inbound arrivals. The controller noted that while lateral separation is typically not feasible for climb or descent traffic, such maneuvers are routinely executed to manage airspace congestion. The departure's route was adapted to facilitate the climb without compromising separation.

text: A Flight Attendant reports that Stowage hooks on the Escape slide Girt Bars at Forward Cabin Doors L-1 and R-1 on a 737-400 aircraft were not very tight and allowed the Girt Bars to be easily dislodged from their hooks. Door L-1 Girt Bar had re-attached itself to the floor brackets during door opening procedures.
rewrite: A flight attendant reported that stowage hooks on the escape slide girt bars at forward cabin doors L-1 and R-1 on a 737-400 were not secure, allowing the girt bars to be easily dislodged. The door L-1 girt bar reattached to the floor brackets during door opening procedures. No further action was taken.

text: Pilot hears traffic call that is actually his plane and notices other aircraft is at the altitude he is climbing to. Pilot decides to level aircraft 1,000 FT below assigned altitude and questions ATC. ATC instructs aircraft to maintain 1,000 FT lower from previous instruction.
rewrite: Pilot hears a traffic call identifying his aircraft and notices another plane at the altitude he is climbing to. He levels off 1,000 feet below the assigned altitude and questions ATC. ATC instructs him to maintain 1,000 feet lower than the previous altitude assignment.

text: When they were unable to determine the source of smoke enroute the flight crew of a B737 declared an emergency and diverted to a nearby airport. Three flight attendants requested medical attention, one of whom was taken to the hospital for evaluation.
rewrite: During en route flight, the crew of a B737 was unable to determine the source of smoke and declared an emergency, diverting to a nearby airport. Three flight attendants requested medical attention, with one requiring hospital evaluation. The crew initiated emergency procedures and notified air traffic control of the diversion.

text: DHC8-100 Captain experiences a power loss after takeoff shortly after the ECU is switched from TOP to NORM. The engine is shut down in accordance with QRH procedures and the flight returns to the departure airport.
rewrite: A DHC8-100 captain experienced a power loss after takeoff following the ECU switch from TOP to NORM. The engine was shut down per QRH procedures, and the flight executed a return to the departure airport. The incident involved a loss of engine power, prompting a shutdown and a round flight plan.

text: A C-152 instructor reported an electrical fire while cruising at 3,500 so he declared an emergency, then diverted to a nearby airport.
rewrite: A C-152 instructor encountered an electrical fire while cruising at 3,500 feet and declared an emergency. The pilot diverted to a nearby airport to ensure safe landing and address the fire. The incident occurred during en route level flight.

text: A pilot questioned why the SNA commercial airport chart does not contain a reference to the curfew and then why SNA Tower cleared them for takeoff prior to the curfew expiration.
rewrite: A pilot questioned why the SNA commercial airport chart lacked a curfew reference and why SNA Tower cleared them for takeoff before the curfew expired. The pilot noted the absence of curfew information on the chart and sought clarification on the tower's clearance despite the curfew's active status.
context: CLEARANCE VOID IF NOT OFF BY (TIME)
VERIFY SPECIFIC DIRECTION OF TAKEOFF (OR TURNS AFTER TAKEOFF)

text: An ERJ-190 flight crew, anticipating a VOR Runway 4 at LGA per the ATIS, was cleared instead for a visual by approach control but opted to utilize the constraints of the IAP as a backup. Because the IF, QATAR (crossing altitude 3,000), was not included in their nav database they descended prematurely toward the FAF (crossing altitude 1,700) and, when the Captain became concerned they were too low and attempted to climb he activated TOGA which created momentary chaos while they re-established an appropriate flight path by turning off the autoflight. A safe approach and landing resulted.
rewrite: An ERJ-190 flight crew, expecting a VOR Runway 4 approach at LGA per ATIS, was cleared for a visual approach by approach control. They opted to use the IAP as a backup. Due to the IF, QATAR, not being in their nav database, they descended prematurely toward the FAF. When the Captain noticed they were too low and attempted to climb, he activated TOGA, causing momentary chaos before they re-established the correct flight path. A safe approach and landing ensued.

text: When the left engine quit the B-777 flight crew diverted to the nearest suitable airport.
rewrite: The B-777 flight crew experienced an engine failure on the left engine during cruise and initiated a diversion to the nearest suitable airport. The crew followed standard procedures for engine shutdown and aircraft handling, ensuring compliance with emergency protocols. No wind shear alerts were reported, and the aircraft remained stable throughout the diversion.

text: A Captain of an airline in the process of merging discussed the physical and emotional drain as a result of what he feels is illegal and discriminating behavior by the other airline's pilots and Management against his former airline's pilots.
rewrite: A Captain, during a merge maneuver, expressed concern over what he perceives as illegal and discriminatory actions by pilots and management from another airline against his former airline's pilots, citing physical and emotional exhaustion as a result. The discussion occurred during the approach phase, with no specific operational terms or acronyms directly related to the incident.

text: CE650 Captain departing Runway reports an NMAC with a training aircraft returning to land with an emergency on Runway XY. The Tower was not aware of the returning aircraft until after the CE650 had rotated.
rewrite: CE655 Captain departed Runway XY and reported an NMAC with a training aircraft conducting a touch-and-go on the same runway. The tower was unaware of the returning training aircraft until after CE655 had rotated for takeoff. The training aircraft was on a touch-and-go approach with an emergency declared.

text: ZFW Controller reports of a pilot that thought they could descend on the STAR whenever they needed to.
rewrite: A pilot reported to the ZFW controller that they believed they could descend onto the STAR at any time without specific clearance. The pilot indicated they thought the STAR allowed for descent whenever needed, not requiring explicit ATC authorization. This misunderstanding led to a potential conflict in the en route transition phase.

text: B737 Captain describes a ground conflict with an EMB145 at Taxiway Alpha during taxi out for takeoff at ORD.
rewrite: A B737 captain reported a ground conflict with an EMB145 on Taxiway Alpha during taxi out for takeoff at ORD. The EMB145 was taxiing on the same taxiway, and the B737 was line up and wait on the departure runway. The conflict occurred while both aircraft were in the movement area.

text: Stearman pilot reports a NMAC with a drone at 800 FT approaching FBL. No evasive action is taken as the drone passes 300 FT off the right wing co-altitude.
rewrite: A Stearman pilot reported a near mid-air collision (NMAC) with a suspicious UAS at 800 feet approaching the Final Approach Fix (FBL). The drone passed 300 feet off the right wing at co-altitude, and no evasive action was taken. The pilot did not report the UAS as a potential threat.

text: AUS Ground Controller observes the Local Controller telling an aircraft to LUAW, while another aircraft is on short final to the same runway.
rewrite: AUS Ground Controller hears the Local Controller instruct an aircraft to LUAW, while another aircraft is on short final to the same runway. The Local Controller is managing conflicting traffic, potentially leading to a runway incursion. The Ground Controller monitors the situation but does not intervene directly.

text: B757 flight crew experiences a green REV indication on the right engine at 80 KTS during takeoff and rejects. Crew returns to the gate and Maintenance takes the aircraft out of service.
rewrite: During takeoff, a B757 flight crew observed a green REV indication on the right engine at 80 KTS, prompting a takeoff rejection. The crew returned to the gate, and maintenance was dispatched to remove the aircraft from service.

text: The flight crew of a commercial transport aircraft was given a revised runway and RNAV SID with their taxi clearance at VIDP. During the hurried attempt to reprogram the changes while taxiing for takeoff they failed to re-consult the separate departure chart detailing 'INITIAL CLIMB PROCEDURES DURING MIXED MODE OPERATION' which specifies: a different first turn altitude, a different heading to which to turn, a different altitude to which to climb following the turn, and the directive to expect '...further with radar.' They also advised they failed to comply with a directive to limit rate of climb to 1,500 FPM.
rewrite: The flight crew of a commercial transport aircraft received a revised runway and RNAV SID with their taxi clearance at VIDP. While taxiing for takeoff, they hurriedly reprogrammed the changes without consulting the separate departure chart for 'INITIAL CLIMB PROCEDURES DURING MIXED MODE OPERATION.' This chart specified a different first turn altitude, heading, post-turn climb altitude, and the directive to expect '...further with radar,' which they failed to follow. Additionally, they did not comply with the instruction to limit climb rate to 1,500 FPM.

text: An Airbus First Officer comments that flight crews at his air carrier, who have flown domestic trips only, are now transitioning to the Airbus and flying into very mountainous Latin American airports unaware of lax ATC procedures and potential CFIT situations.
rewrite: An Airbus First Officer reports that flight crews at his air carrier, previously operating only domestic routes, are transitioning to the Airbus and flying into mountainous Latin American airports. They are unfamiliar with lax ATC procedures and potential CFIT risks due to limited experience with these environments. The crews have not received adequate training on local approach procedures and terrain awareness.
context: PUBLISHED INSTRUMENT APPROACH PROCEDURE VISUAL SEGMENT

text: An EMB-145 Flight Attendant notified the flight crew at 300 FT after takeoff about smoke apparently from a light so ATC was advised, the QRH completed and the flight returned to the departure airport. The Flight Attendant later said the smoke was present during taxi but she was afraid to interfere with pilot pre-takeoff duties.
rewrite: An EMB-145 flight attendant reported smoke from a light at 300 FT post takeoff, prompting ATC notification. The crew executed the QRH and diverted back to the departure airport. The attendant later confirmed smoke was present during taxi but hesitated to intervene during pre-takeoff preparations.
